title: From stable high costs to variable low costs: A continuum of non‐breeding energy expenditure strategies in North Atlantic seabirds
content:
North Atlantic pelagic seabirds adopt a continuum of non-breeding energetic strategies, arising from variable movement and thermoregulation costs. Individuals trade off temporal variability in energy expenditure with cumulative costs, with consequences for resource demand and sensitivity to changing seascapes.


Abstract

In the wild, many animals track shifting resource availability, a capacity with profound implications for fitness and population viability. Mobile species capable of long-distance movement can access a variety of habitats when not breeding, driving individuals to employ distinct behavioural strategies as they move through environments with contrasting effects on energetic costs (e.g. locomotion or thermoregulation) or gains (e.g. food intake). How energy expenditure is managed during this period may influence the degree to which individuals must accommodate variable resource demand, while its accumulation over time may affect how easily individuals rebuild condition ahead of reproduction. Using light-level geolocation-immersion loggers, we modelled the coefficient of variation in weekly (WEECOV_NB; reflecting stable vs. variable energy expenditure) and total (TEENB) non-breeding season energy expenditure for 8 to 33 North Atlantic populations of six pelagic seabird species contrasting in movement ability and distribution. Within-species, we tested for population differences in WEECOV_NB and TEENB, and, within-individuals, a link between the two (i.e. whether periods of above-average weekly energy expenditure, WEE, accumulate over time or are offset by periods of below-average WEE, leading to lower TEENB). Between-population differences in WEECOV_NB and TEENB were strongest in diving species with high flight costs, where both metrics increased with decreasing individual encountered sea surface temperature (a driver of thermoregulatory costs) and WEECOV_NB increased with individual migratory distance (two diving species only). We further identified a continuum of energy expenditure strategies, with individuals of all species except northern fulmars spanning low TEENB–high WEECOV_NB to high TEENB–low WEECOV_NB. This suggests that multiple energetic pathways for navigating the non-breeding season are possible in this marine region. Ultimately, these analyses underscore energetic trade-offs shaping non-breeding season movement strategies, with implications for energy demand and fitness. As energy expenditure must be matched by intake, non-breeding seabirds in the North Atlantic likely differ in the magnitude and timing of resource requirement. These populations may thus differ in their vulnerability to stressors that further elevate costs or reduce access to prey and in their capacity to cope with environmental change.
